Before you begin

Getting started

Speaking Plants shows the data of instrumented coffee plants: soil, leaf and air sensors, sent every 5 minutes through a LoRa radio gateway. It works without Internet.

  1. Open the dashboard. On the field computer, double-click Lancer-station-terrain.bat (Windows) or run Rscript scripts/run_field_station.R. The window prints the address to open, for example http://localhost:3838. From a phone or tablet on the same Wi-Fi, use the network address it prints.
  2. Read the tabs from left to right. Status tells you if everything is fine right now; the analysis tabs (Overview to Quality) explain what happened; Alerts and Sync are for the person in charge.
  3. Watch the light at the top right. It summarises all plants: normal, warning, critical. Click it to go back to Status.
About the screenshotsThe screenshots in this guide come from a test run with the gateway simulator, so the plants are marked SIMULATED. Simulated data are never measurements. The soil moisture sensor in use today is preliminary, so its values are for testing, not for irrigation decisions.
Left panel

The sidebar: choosing the data

The sidebar decides which data the analysis tabs (Overview, Time Series, Thermal, Stress, Quality, Alerts history, Download) show.

  1. Choose the source at the top: File to upload a CSV (or Load bundled sample dataset), or Database for the data received from the gateway.
  2. Read the summary box: number of plants (the red badge counts simulated ones), records, file size and last record. Click Recent imports to see what was added or refused as a duplicate.
  3. Pick a Plant ("(simulated)" marks demonstration plants; All plants loads them all) and a Period: 24 h, 3, 7 or 30 days, Everything, or Custom range.
  4. Untick Include thermal frames to load long periods faster. Keep Live ticked to see new data arrive without reloading.
  5. Click Load from database. The box below confirms what is loaded.
  6. Lower down, the Time window slider narrows every tab to part of the period (buttons Last 12 h, 6 h, 1 h).
Tab 1

Status | is everything all right now?

One card per plant with a traffic light. It always shows the latest readings, whatever is loaded in the sidebar.

  1. Station strip (top): files waiting in the gateway inbox, imported today and rejected; last synchronisation with the cloud.
  2. Plant cards, worst first. The big light and the word (NORMAL, WARNING, CRITICAL) give the plant's state: the worst of its rules.
  3. Rule lines inside the card: each rule has its own small light and the current value. Bold lines are the ones causing the alert. Here, sim_node_B is yellow because its soil is drying; sim_node_C because its battery and radio signal are weak.
  4. View data opens the Overview tab on that plant's last 24 hours.
  5. Inactive and archived plants (click to unfold) lists plants silent for more than 24 h and the demonstration archive; they are not counted in the alerts.
LightMeaningWhat to do
NormalWithin the comfortable rangeNothing
WarningOutside the comfortable rangeWatch it, check the plant
CriticalOutside the safe range, or a node silent for more than 1 hAct: irrigate, shade, check the equipment
No dataThis plant does not measure itNothing
TipThe page updates by itself when new data arrive and every minute. Plant rules use the average of the last 15 minutes, so one odd reading does not trigger an alert.
Tab 2

Overview | the latest values on one page

A summary of the data chosen in the sidebar.

  1. Banners: red Simulated data when the plant is simulated; orange reminder that soil moisture comes from a preliminary sensor; red if a sensor shows the same value all the time.
  2. Latest measurement: soil moisture and temperature, leaf and air temperature, humidity, pressure, and the leaf – air difference.
  3. Dataset: number of records and completeness, median interval between records (should be 5 min), length of the period, number of gaps.
  4. Lower down: a small temperature chart and the list of variables found.
Tab 3

Time Series |how did the values change?

Draw any variable over time, zoom on a period, compare leaf and air.

  1. Tick the variables in the left panel, or use the quick buttons Leaf, Air, Soil, Clear.
  2. Layout: Single panel for variables with the same unit (temperatures); One panel per variable to mix temperature, humidity and pressure.
  3. Overlay rolling mean adds a smoothed trend line.
  4. Zoom: drag across the chart, or move the handles of the small slider below it. Double-click to zoom out. Hover a curve to read the exact value.
  5. The second chart, Leaf temperature versus air temperature, shows the leaf (with its min–max band) and the air on the same axis. When the leaf rises above the air, the plant is transpiring less.
Tab 4

Thermal | the heat image of the leaves

The MLX90640 camera sees the plant as 32 × 24 = 768 temperature points. This tab rebuilds the image for each record.

  1. Choose the moment with the Frame slider, step with |< < > >|, or press ▶ to play the images as an animation.
  2. Read the cards: coldest pixel, average, hottest pixel, and their range.
  3. Read the image: dark red is cooler, yellow-white is warmer. A transpiring leaf stays cool; hot patches can mean stress, sun on the leaf, or the pot behind the foliage.
  4. Colour scale: Fixed across all frames to compare moments; Auto-fit to this frame to see detail in one image.
  5. Camera orientation: mirror or rotate once so the image matches the plant. The histogram on the right shows how many pixels sit at each temperature.
Tab 5

Stress | is the plant short of water?

Three simple indicators computed from the measurements. Each formula is written on screen.

IndicatorFormulaHow to read it
Leaf – air temperature differenceleaf average − air averageAt or below 0, the leaf cools itself by transpiring. Above 0 and rising, it transpires less: a classic sign of water stress.
Leaf temperature rangeleaf max − leaf minSpread of temperature in the camera view. A relative index.
Soil – air temperature differencesoil − air averageThe soil buffers the air; this swings opposite to the daily air cycle.
  1. The cards give the latest value, the mean over the window and the range.
  2. Indicators over time: tick or untick each indicator, zoom as in Time Series. Look at the midday hours: that is when stress shows.
  3. Lower down: the mean daily pattern by hour, and the leaf – air difference against humidity.
Interpretation limitsOne plant and a preliminary soil sensor are enough to test the dashboard, not to diagnose the crop.
Tab 6

Fields | when to irrigate each plot

A FAO-56 water balance per field plot (rain, evaporation, crop, soil) that says which plots need water. A decision aid, not a measurement.

  1. Bring in the plots: Import a GeoJSON or CSV file, Load demonstration fields, or Add a field by coordinates.
  2. Describe the crop and soil: crop, soil texture, planting date, irrigation system.
  3. Choose the weather source: Bundled demonstration data works offline; Open-Meteo needs Internet; Copernicus ERA5-Land needs an account. Set the days of history and forecast.
  4. Click Compute advice, then read the cards: plots to irrigate now, to monitor, without stress, and the water required in m³.
  5. Lower down: a map of the plots, the tables Field status and Advice by field. Click a row to see that plot's water balance.
TipIrrigation is due when the line reaches the dashed threshold. The satellite comparison is only a cross-check: one satellite pixel covers 9 to 11 km.
Tab 7

Quality | can the data be trusted?

Check completeness before reading any curve.

  1. Warnings (top): red for gaps longer than the expected 5 minutes (here the longest is 365 min, a 6-hour outage); orange for short intervals and missing values.
  2. Cards: completeness, missing values, missing thermal pixels, duplicate timestamps removed, intervals within 300 s ± 30 s.
  3. Column validation: Info on optional columns only means this plant does not measure them (for example the node battery).
  4. Observed sampling intervals: rows marked Gap or Short point to logger or radio problems.
  5. Lower down: interval chart, missing values per variable, duplicates, and the list of every gap with its start and end.
Tab 8

Alerts | setting the limits and reading the history

The limits that turn values green, yellow or red, and the history of alerts in the loaded data.

  1. A value below Critical low or above Critical high is red; below Warning low or above Warning high is yellow; otherwise green. Example: air temperature 10 / 15 / 28 / 32 °C.
  2. Type a new number in a box to change a limit. Leave a box empty to disable that limit. Untick On to switch the rule off.
  3. Click Save rules. Limits must increase from left to right, otherwise the app says which rule is wrong. Discard changes returns to the saved values; Restore defaults brings back the original ones (then Save).
  4. The Why column explains each default value. Saved rules apply to everyone using this computer.
  1. The history colours every record of the data loaded in the sidebar, rule by rule. The table lists each warning or critical episode with its start, end and number of records.
Default limitsThe default values are starting points for Coffea arabica. They must be validated by the agronomy team for each site.
Tab 9

Sync | gateway in, cloud out

Follow the data coming from the LoRa gateway and going to the cloud.

  1. Gateway inbox: files waiting, imported today, rejected. Scan inbox now imports at once. A green dot means imported; a rejected file goes to inbox/rejected with the reason.
  2. Synchronisation status: role of this computer, cloud target, packages waiting, last successful send. Sync now sends immediately; Test connection checks the cloud without sending.
  3. Station and cloud settings (set once): station name, role (Field station or Web platform), cloud target (Synced folder such as Google Drive or OneDrive, or WebDAV such as Nextcloud), sync frequency. Click Save settings.
  4. Manual transfer when there is no connection: choose Records not yet synced or All records, click Download transfer file, carry it on a USB key or by e-mail, then use Import transfer files on the other computer.
  5. The journal at the bottom lists every package sent or received and its status.
Nothing is lost offlineNew records wait in the outbox folder and leave by themselves when the connection returns. Sending the same data twice is harmless: duplicates are refused.
Tab 10

Download | taking the data away

CSV exports of the plant and time window chosen in the sidebar.

ExportWhat you get
Cleaned datasetEvery record, sorted, duplicates removed, with the three stress indicators. Tick the box to add the 768 pixel columns.
Summary statisticsFor each variable: count, missing, mean, standard deviation, min, quartiles, median, max.
Data quality reportColumn checks, missing values, intervals and every gap, in one file.
Thermal framesMin, mean and max of each heat image, or the image on screen as a 24 × 32 grid.
Simulated files are labelledWhen simulated data are shown, file names start with SIMULATED_ and the data carry an is_simulated column.
Reference

Glossary

TermMeaning
RecordOne line of data: one plant, one 5-minute interval.
LoRa gatewayThe radio receiver that collects the sensor messages and writes them as files into the inbox folder.
Inbox / outboxFolder where data arrive / folder where packages wait to be sent.
RuleA set of limits that turns a value into green, yellow or red.
Transfer packageA compressed, sealed file of new records, ready to be sent or carried on a USB key.
Web platformThe online copy of the dashboard that receives the packages of all stations.
Preliminary sensorThe current soil moisture sensor, not yet calibrated: it can raise a warning, never a critical alert.
Simulated dataGenerated data used to test the dashboard; always marked SIMULATED, never measurements.
